title: Active Listening

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Someone gives you directions to their house. Passive listening is standing there nodding. Active listening is saying, 'So I turn left at the gas station, then go two blocks?' Now they can answer 'yes' or 'no, three blocks.' That checking-back step is what makes listening active: you prove you got the message instead of hoping you did.

### Question 2

Before you can catch a ball, you have to face the thrower and put down whatever is in your hands. Attending is that step. Nothing has been caught yet and nothing has been said back, but you have made yourself physically and mentally available so the rest of listening can actually work.

### Question 3

Think of a campfire. Minimal encouragers are gentle puffs of air on the coals: enough to keep the fire going, not enough to move it or change what is burning. A nod or an 'mm-hmm' adds no new content and asks no new question, so the speaker keeps their place while still knowing you are there.

### Question 4

Sending a message with no feedback is like throwing a paper airplane and walking away: you never learn where it landed. Active listening turns it into playing catch. You throw the meaning back, and the other person sees whether you caught the right thing, so a small misunderstanding gets fixed while it is still small.

### Question 5

Your brain can take in words far faster than anyone can say them, like a race car stuck behind a bicycle. All that extra speed has to go somewhere, so it wanders off to dinner plans. Active listening gives the race car a job, such as sorting what you hear into main points, so the extra speed works on the conversation instead of away from it.

### Question 6

Listening has different jobs. When someone gives you directions, the job is getting details right, so you repeat street names back. When a friend is upset, the job is understanding how they feel, and repeating street names would be useless. Same ears, different job, different moves. Naming the job first tells you which listening move to make.

### Question 7

Try writing a note while someone reads you a phone number. The instant you start writing, you stop hearing digits. Planning your reply mid-conversation does the same thing: the words keep arriving, but the part of you that was catching them is now busy building an answer instead.

### Question 8

When someone hands you a tangled ball of string, the useful move is to hold it up and say, 'so this end goes here, and this part is knotted,' and let them tell you whether you have it right. Option D holds the string up. The others hand it straight back with advice, comfort, or a measurement, before anyone has looked at it.

### Question 9

On a long drive you do not wait four hours to check whether you are on the right road; you check at each exit. Summarizing aloud is checking at the exit: 'here is what I think we have agreed so far.' If you are off course, you find out one exit later instead of at the end of the trip.

### Question 10

If a friend says 'I'm not cold' while shivering, you have two pieces of information, not one. Ignoring the shivering wastes half of it; announcing that they are contradicting themselves makes them defend the words. Saying 'you said you're fine, but you seem down, want to tell me more?' hands both pieces back and lets them decide which one to explain.

### Question 11

Picture a friend who says 'that's so interesting!' after everything you say, in exactly the same voice every time. The words are right, but you stop believing them and start saying less. Reflecting someone's words only works when it comes out of actually paying attention; otherwise it sounds like a recording, and people can hear the difference.

### Question 12

Imagine sorting mail into 'junk' and 'important' after reading only the first line of each envelope. Once something is labeled junk, you stop reading it carefully, even if page two had a check in it. Holding the label until the whole message is in keeps you from discarding the part that mattered. You still judge; you just judge last.
